extracted.intended_audience: early childhood education researchers, preschool teachers, and practitioners interested in children's humour development
extracted.subtask_description: Qualitative (phenomenological) research examining how 60–72-month-old children produce and appreciate humour and how their teachers describe children's humour and humour styles. Includes instrument development, data collection with drawings/interviews, coding, and interpretation using established humour theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: McGhee’s Humour Development Stages
rubrics_metrics.description: McGhee defined humour development in four stages: incongruous actions towards objects (18–20 months), incongruous labelling of objects and events (20–24 months), conceptual incongruity (2–7 years), and humour with multiple meanings (7–11 years). The 60–72-month-olds in this study were assumed to be in the third stage (conceptual incongruity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual incongruity: children make jokes about themselves and others, produce abstract/complex jokes, are aware of 'violations of the perceptual appearances of things' (McGhee, 1984, p.230). Use this staging to interpret what types of humour children appreciate and produce at given ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martin’s Humour Styles Theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Martin (2007) presents four humour styles: two adaptive (self-enhancing — positive humour toward self; affiliative — positive humour toward others) and two maladaptive (self-defeating — negative humour toward self; aggressive — negative humour toward others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptive styles promote pro-social behaviours, self-confidence and social acceptance; maladaptive styles (self-defeating, aggressive) can damage self-esteem or relationships and may result in social rejection. Use this framework to categorise socio-emotional functions of children's humour and teachers' descriptions of children's humour behaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation Form of Humorous Factors in Children's Books — Pictorial Humour Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial humour types (from Johnson, 2010) include: objects with incongruous features, physical deformities, caricature and exaggeration, masks, clowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these pictorial categories to code visual/illustrative elements that provoke humour (e.g., unusual physical features, caricatured expressions, exaggeration). In this study these categories were used to analyse children's drawings and responses to illustrated books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation Form of Humorous Factors in Children's Books — Verbal Humour Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal humour types (from Johnson, 2010) include: non-language sounds, nonsense words, rhyming, erroneous labelling of objects, joke telling, repetitious rhyming, slapstick, puns, knock-knock jokes, irony, satire, riddles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these verbal categories when analysing children's verbal productions or explanations of humour (e.g., nonsense words, puns). Although this study focused on drawings and pictorial humour, the verbal types form part of the evaluation instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation Form of Humorous Factors in Children's Books — Situational Humour Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Situational humour types (from Johnson, 2010) include: pretend play with objects, tickling and body contact, mastered skills, body parts and potty humour, pranks and mischief, clumsiness, teasing, social mistakes by peers, practical jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use situational categories to code humour emerging from actions, social interactions, and events (e.g., pranks, teasing). The authors used these to categorise elements found in children's drawings and explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age-to-humour-type mapping (Table 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping of ages to humour types: 1–2 years (McGhee Stage 1 & 2; Piaget sensorimotor) associated with simple pictorial/verbal/situational types; 2–7 years (McGhee Stage 3; Piaget preoperational) associated with conceptual incongruity; 7+ years (McGhee Stage 4; Piaget concrete operations) associated with humour with multiple meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the age-stage mapping to anticipate which humour types children are likely to appreciate or produce. The study assumed 60–72-month-old children sit within the conceptual incongruity stage (2–7 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors included in 'funny' drawing — coding categories and codes (Table 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories used to code children's drawings: Conceptual incongruity, Physical deformity, Caricature, Exaggeration, Costume. Example codes: big/little people; giving human features to unloving things; giving animal features to people; unusual physical features; unusual combination of things; unusual size and number of body parts; unusual shape/colour of body parts; hurting somebody else; unusual/unappropriated behaviours of things; exaggerated number of things; exaggerated little or big size of things; clown; nurse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the concrete coding labels applied to children’s drawings to identify what elements children considered funny. Use the listed codes when classifying pictorial elements in children's produced drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers' categories for describing students' humour behaviours (Table 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher-reported categories: Maladaptive Humour (e.g., uses physical humour that affects relationships negatively), Adaptive Humour (e.g., likes to laugh and make jokes; uses humour on his/her own; shares humour with others; reflects usual things in a funny way), No Humour (does not use humour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify teachers' qualitative descriptions of children's humour in classroom contexts and to link observed behaviours to Martin's adaptive/maladaptive distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument development and selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview questions were developed after literature review, pilot study and expert opinions (three professors). The Evaluation Form of Humorous Factors in Children's Books (Johnson, 2010) adapted to Turkish was used to choose a humorous illustration from ~80 books; five illustrations from each category were considered and the final illustration chosen based on expert opinions and children's reactions in pilot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruments with literature grounding, obtain expert review, pilot-test with target-age participants, and use iterative elimination with both expert and child feedback when selecting stimuli (e.g., book illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Child-appropriate data collection procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures included: using a story-reading component and props to build rapport; replacing term 'humorous illustration' with 'funny' for child comprehension; having teacher present to ensure comfort; reading story and then asking children to draw (to avoid influence); asking children to explain drawings in one-on-one interviews in a quiet part of classroom; audio-recording and researcher note-taking; separate room for one-on-one interviews about book illustrations; typical durations: 30–40 minutes for story/drawing/interview, 10–15 minutes per one-on-one child interview, 10–15 minutes per teacher interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching young children, use age-appropriate language, rapport-building (stories, props), ensure comfort (teacher present), sequence tasks to avoid priming (drawing before showing illustration), use audio-recording and notes, and allocate short, child-suitable interview durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion and exclusion criteria for children's drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Included: drawings created by participant children who wanted to share, and drawings that considered the 'funniness' concept and were connected to the story. Excluded: drawings not connected to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include artefacts that are produced in-task and relevant to the study prompt; exclude off-task or unrelated productions to preserve construct validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data analysis and coding procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Audio-recordings were transcribed; main points were coded. Deductive coding was used (codes developed before analysis). Two coders (the first author and another researcher; both hold master's degrees in early childhood education) performed coding; almost all codes matched — some wording replaced by more generic terms to facilitate understanding. Codes were determined using Johnson's Evaluation Form for children's data and Martin's humour styles for teachers' views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive coding tied to established instruments/theory; employ at least two trained coders, check for code matching, reconcile differences, and consider generic rewording for clarity. Use transcription, memoing, and note-taking to preserve context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and consent procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethical permissions obtained from a state university Ethics Committee and the Turkish Ministry of National Education. Parental written consent was required; children were verbally asked for willingness to participate; confidentiality assurances given; audio recording permitted by participants; teacher presence used to create comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure institutional ethics approvals and relevant governmental permissions, obtain informed parental consent and child assent, ensure confidentiality, and gain explicit permission for audio-recording. Use procedures appropriate to minors and local regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complementary theoretical frameworks for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used both McGhee’s humour development theory (to interpret children's humour development and to apply categories of conceptual incongruity) and Martin’s humour styles (to interpret socio-emotional aspects and teachers' descriptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine developmental and socio-emotional theoretical lenses to provide richer interpretations: use McGhee for age-stage conceptual coding and Martin for adaptive/maladaptive social-function coding of humour.
